summary:
Visitors to Kentucky stand under the United States federal framework on travel documents and screening. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, defined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary and barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity; the State Department stopped processing the X marker, new passports are issued only as M or F according to supporting documents, and passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until expiry. The Supreme Court allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect in November 2025, superseding a State Department policy dating to 1992. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, and the ACLU is suing the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs. Airport screening carries an outing risk through secondary screening, devices and pat-downs, and visa discretion applies on arrival in Kentucky as anywhere else in the country, including the February 2025 bar on trans athletes entering to compete in women's sports and the treatment of listing a gender other than assigned sex as grounds for a permanent fraud-based ban.

Kentucky is one of the states that restrict which bathrooms transgender people may use. A Movement Advancement Project tally counts state bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings in nine states and one territory, with 29 states, four territories and the District of Columbia having no such ban. Kentucky's 2023 K-12 facility ban appears among the map's state-by-state entries, and it rests on a single statute: Senate Bill 150, enacted on 29 March 2023 when the Kentucky legislature overrode Governor Andy Beshear's veto.

Senate Bill 150 restricts which bathrooms transgender students can use in public schools and also bans gender-affirming medical care for transgender minors in Kentucky. The Kentucky Department of Education issued guidance in April 2023 for school districts implementing the state's 2023 rules, advising districts to tread cautiously with the bathroom-ban provisions; the districts themselves carry out the facility restriction, so its application varies from school to school.

The care prohibition took effect on 14 July 2023, when U.S. District Judge David Hale lifted the injunction he had issued the previous month, preventing transgender minors in Kentucky from accessing puberty blockers and hormone therapy. Seven transgender children and their parents had sued to block the law; the ACLU of Kentucky called the ruling a temporary setback. Executive Order 14187 of January 2025 described gender-affirming care for minors as "chemical and surgical mutilation of children," some hospitals paused care, and in summer 2025 the Department of Justice subpoenaed over 20 hospitals for full records of patients under 19. Several of these federal measures have been blocked or enjoined in court.
tangentialFactors:
Gender-affirming care for children is banned in 27 states, so Kentucky's 2023 statute sits inside a wider state-level pattern rather than an isolated rule. Facility restrictions are equally widespread and are tightening: some states make trans bathroom use a criminal offence in certain circumstances, and in April 2025 a transgender student was arrested and handcuffed in a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol, which civil-rights attorneys described as the first known arrest under that state's bathroom-restriction law.

Document rules in other states have moved further than Kentucky's. In February 2026 Kansas enacted a law preventing transgender people from changing markers on birth certificates and driver's licences, invalidating existing documents that do not match sex assigned at birth, and barring trans people from sex-segregated facilities; rights groups call it a template for other states. A July 2026 national risk assessment flagged Idaho as the latest "Do Not Travel" state for trans people, bringing the total to four, and reported that the 2026 legislative season continued to degrade trans rights.

Foreign governments have responded to US document and data rules. In April 2025 CNN reported that several countries issued advisories about trans people travelling to the United States, and Axios reported in March 2025 that at least eight European countries, including Finland and Denmark, adjusted travel guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens entering the US.

Federal custody and enforcement present documented harm relevant to anyone entering the country. From 2026 the Federal Bureau of Prisons adopted policies mandating conversion therapy for transgender inmates, including cutting hair short, withdrawing hormone medication and substituting psychiatric therapy, while the Bureau stopped reporting the number of transgender prisoners held from 2025. In December 2025 the Attorney General instructed the FBI to offer cash bounties for information leading to the identification and arrest of transgender activists described as promoting "radical gender ideology"; a May 2026 White House counterterrorism strategy prioritised groups whose ideology is "anti-American, radically pro-transgender, and anarchist." Advocates have compared these actions to the early stages of genocide.
localsOnly:
The 2023 statute governs Kentucky residents as well as visitors, but its operative reach for adults outside schools is not established by these sources: Senate Bill 150's facility provision is written around public schools, where districts implement it under Kentucky Department of Education guidance issued in April 2023.

Residents who are minors face the care prohibition directly. Since 14 July 2023 transgender minors in Kentucky have been barred from puberty blockers and hormone therapy, and the litigation brought by seven transgender children and their parents did not prevent the ban from taking effect.

Trans adults in Kentucky obtain identity documents under state procedures that these sources do not describe; no sourced Kentucky rule on birth-certificate or driver's-licence sex markers appears in this record. Nor is there a sourced Kentucky hate-crime statute or statewide nondiscrimination provision covering gender identity.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: whether Senate Bill 150's facility provision has been amended, narrowed by litigation, or expanded since 2023, and whether the 2023 care ban remains in force without further injunction, are not established by the available sources.

Unresolved: Kentucky's rules for changing sex markers on birth certificates and driver's licences are not sourced here, so the record cannot state whether a visitor's or resident's state-issued identification will match federal passport markers.

Unresolved: the scope of adult restroom and facility access outside public schools under Kentucky law is not sourced, as is any state-level criminal penalty for trans facility use.

Not sourced: the outcome of the ACLU of Kentucky's challenge beyond the 14 July 2023 lifting of the injunction, and whether appeals followed.
